  "text": "## Introduction
Stroke is a major health problem, not only due to the mortality rate, but also for its effects on motor and cognitive ability, and on the quality of life of survivors and their family. Patients' neurological handicaps are often severe and profound, expressed through many incapacities: locomotion, communication, self-care, behaviour, physical independence, orientation, social and economic integration (Fodor et al., 2018). The inability to move independently, along with the regaining of speed (gait) in walking, is two determining factors of long-term disability and alteration of daily-life functions (Mauritz, 2002).

Even with optimal care in specialized units, less than a third of patients having suffered a stroke will ever fully recover (The Atlantis et al., 2004). Following a stroke, patients are prescribed a complex and individualized recovery plan that is unlimited in time, begins in the intensive care unit and later continues in a medical recovery clinic or at the patient's home. Recovery treatment aims to give stroke-disabled patients the opportunity to maintain their physical, intellectual, psychological and social functions at an optimal level (International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, 2014). Recent clinical studies question the use of multiple classes of drugs to treat disabilities resulting from stroke, findings corroborated by physiotherapeutic and occupational approaches (Keskin et al., 2005).

Mainly due to the perspectives of application and theoretic importance, the last decade has seen a step forward in neurotrophic factors which now occupy a leading position in scientific research. To date, no specific schemes, medicines or definitive methods have emerged to treat the consequences of a stroke (Uivaroşan et al., 2018). Rehabilitation and reintegration of stroke patients should be undertaken with consideration for the type of disease that caused the deficiency and focus on disability reduction and management. However, since the recovery program is set up in function of diagnosis, the latter is critical (Fodor et al., 2018). Though the post-stroke recovery program may evolve for improved results, its impact on motor function remains modest, regardless of the method applied (Mauritz, 2002). One of the most discussed features of gait recovery is that the patient must be as actively involved in the rehabilitation program as possible. This ultimately request implies better learning of the motor process, but it may also reduce the incidence of secondary complications such as cardiovascular disease or osteoporosis. Inability to move is a long-term handicap and is considered a key target in rehabilitation (Mauritz, 2002).

For the greatest possible improvement of motor function, we have studied the use of robotic techniques and devices for gait recovery (Cho et al., 2018; Lunenburger et al., 2005) and a number of therapeutic benefits have come to our attention: increased independence (Cho et al., 2018; Dundar et al., 2014), improved walking (Simons et al., 2009), muscle tone (Schwartz et al., 2009), walking speed, mobility, etc. (Schwartz et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2006). Among the advantages of using medical robots are dynamic workout programs whose aim is to improve patient condition by reproducing exercises otherwise performed by specialized physical therapists and by quantifying the results. One of the robotic devices used to rehabilitate walking is the Lokomat, a computer-controlled and electrically-driven orthosis for walking, designed to assist training by means of a conveyor belt (Pohl et al., 2007). The Lokomat supports the walking movement, using a physiological walking pattern to guide the patient's legs, with body-weight support as an option. It provides all the benefits of a robotic locomotor workout, training features, research and evaluation facilities, and hand-assisted training. Study of the medical robot therapy useful in restoring gait showed that better recovery is possible if the therapy is prompt, intense and prolonged (Cho et al., 2018; Lunenburger et al., 2005). Some data have demonstrated that the potential of robotic therapy is greater in the early stages following a stroke (Álvarez et al., 2000; Alvarez et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2017). Other researches have shown that, in certain cases, robotic techniques may be more effective than conventional therapy (Hesse and Werner, 2009; Israel et al., 2006; Peurala et al., 2009). However, there are some published papers mentioning that walking behaviour with devices that maximize the level of motor support (such as Lokomat) does not always produce positive results (Hidler et al., 2009a, 2009b; Maulden et al., 2005; Pohl et al., 2007); moreover, some data show that the effects of using this type of device on walking function, including the motor recovery after subacute stroke, still remain unclear (Cho et al., 2018).

At present, the therapeutic approach for post-stroke rehabilitation involves use of multiple therapies that act in different but complementary ways to identify treatment schemes that transform disabilities into abilities. The advantages of robotic devices, along with the benefits of neurotrophic medication and standard recovery procedures, led us to hypothesize that a combination of these therapies could improve both functional recovery and the quality of life. Thus, our aim was to study the effects of Lokomat use on stroke victims when used: 1) in combination with both Cerebrolysin and recovery therapy, 2) when associated only with classic recovery therapy.

## Study design
A comparative prospective study was conducted involving seventy Romanian patients having suffered a stroke within the previous 6 months, and who were hospitalized for post-stroke recovery at the Recovery Clinic Hospital of Băile Felix and at the Oradea Neurology Hospital during the 2011–2014 period. Observation and treatment were programed for 12 months, with initial evaluation, at 6 months and at 12 months. To determine the efficacy of Lokomat training associated with neurotrophic medication and the classic balneo-physiotherapeutic recovery treatment for stroke patients, we compared three parallel groups: Group I (n = 22) – Lokomat combined with balneo-physiotherapy and Cerebrolysin; Group II (n = 18) – Lokomat associated only with balneo-physiotherapy; and Group III (n = 30) – balneo-physiotherapy alone (Control group). Patients who participated in the study were distributed among the 3 groups considering the selection method for each group along with to the patient's history, associated pathologies, clinical characteristics, and the signed consent for training with Lokomat. Only hemodynamically stable patients with no risks of vital importance were included in the study.

The patients were evaluated physically, neurologically and functionally, following the evolution of pyramidal spasticity, functional independence and their health-related quality of life. In the initial assessment, and in terms of the parameters evaluated, no statistically significant differences between the groups (p > 0.05) were observed.

The study was approved by the Ethics Commission of the Council of the Medicine and Pharmacy Faculty, University of Oradea, and conducted in accordance with the World Medical Association Code of Ethics (Declaration of Helsinki, 1967). Each patient included in the study signed an informed-consent form.

## Drug/medicinal therapy
Cerebrolysin was administered as a chronic intermittent treatment in doses of 10 mL/day, 10 consecutive days per month, for one year. It was administered intravenously as an infusion, diluted in a physiological saline solution. During the study, treatment with medicines belonging to the following classes was allowed: antihypertensives, antidiabetics, antibiotics, hydro-electrolytic and acid-base rebalancing, thrombolytic, and general stroke treatment. Throughout the study, no treatment with different neuroprotectors was administered, excepting diazepam, amantadine, cistoline or piracetam (which act peripherally), or pentoxifylline, nicergoline, vinpocetine, Ginkgo biloba or vincamine (which determine blood vessel dilatation).

## Recovery therapy
Recovery treatment, with established procedures, was performed for 14 (consecutive) days, every 6 months and was strictly individualized, regardless of stroke type (thrombotic, embolic, haemorrhagic), and took into account age, associated conditions, risk factors, degree and form of motor deficiency, complications etc. Therapeutic means used were: • kinetotherapy, using a variety of postures, techniques and methods, types of exercises and passive, active or active-passive exercises; • hydrokinetotherapy by immersing the patient in thermal water at 36–37 °C in collective pools, especially in swimming pools, under the strict supervision of a physical therapist; • masotherapy, using adapted and strictly individualized massage techniques, performed either in the ward/salon or in a massage room; • electrotherapy using low, medium or high frequency currents, depending on the level of spasticity, on presence/existence of complications such as joint or musculo-ligament retractions or associated pathology of the locomotor apparatus; • occupational therapy for the performance of ADL by self-care, domestic, professional and social care in relation to the patient's life stage; • thermotherapy, in the form of dose III short waves, to reduce spasticity; • cryotherapy in various forms, applied either to decrease spasticity or, in stage II, to relieve lymphatic circulation; • contrasting therapy in the form of alternating baths of the upper or lower limbs, aimed to improve venous circulation; • psychotherapy performed individually by a psychologist.

In all groups, kinetotherapy and massage were performed for all patients, hydro-kinetotherapy was performed for over 50% of patients. Electrotherapy, with various forms of low and high frequency currents, was applied to 72–74% of patients, and occupational therapy was applied to 83–86% of patients. No significant differences (p > 0.05) concerning the rehabilitation treatments were observed between the studied groups.

## Lokomat training
Lokomat is a robot assisted training/rehabilitation system consisting of a treadmill, a dynamic body weight support system and robotic (motorized) orthoses that allow patients with severe locomotor deficiency to train their walking using a physiological model of walking. This device facilitates symmetrical walking patterns of hip and knee components using an exoskeleton powered by programmable servomotors (Bae et al., 2014). During training, patients are supported by harnesses to stay safe on the treadmill; they begin their workout training using the body weight support system and the motorized orthosis.

Throughout the training, therapists can control the speed of walking, the angle of the knee and hip joints, and the amount of physical support provided by the body weight support system. Walking training sessions are kept at a demanding level; the speed of the treadmill is set at the maximum that patients tolerate, the force of the acting mechanisms is adjusted, and support for body weight is reduced as soon as the functionality of the patients accepts and supports it. All patients in this study were trained at Lokomat while they were admitted to the recovery clinic, as follows: 30 min/day, for 14 consecutive days, every 6 months.

## Spasticity assessment
The adapted Ashworth scale, a standard scale showing resistance to/endurance of inactive movement, was used to evaluate levels of pyramidal spasticity. The procedure offers the examiner continuous observation of the endurance stage. A scale of severity degrees from 0 to 4 includes 5 muscle tone stages. The scale suggested by Bahanon adds level 1 + (Modified Ashworth Scale, 2011).

## Motor deficiency evaluation – Barthel Index
The Barthel Index, which tests 10 stages for using the 10 ADL for self-care was used to evaluate motor deficiency. The index applies to all 10 assessed functions (Barthel Index Scoring Form, 2011).

## Functional independence evaluation
To evaluate functional independence, the FIM scale (Functional Independence Measure) was used, a standard measuring system that contains 6 parameters. Functional independence is presented on a decreasing scale in 7 stages, from 7 (totally independent) to 1 (totally dependent) (Cavanagh et al., 2000). A high score indicates a healthy individual with no dysfunctionalities.

## Quality of life evaluation
To evaluate quality of life, the SS-QoL scale (Stroke Specific Quality of Life Scale) was used, a standard scale to evaluate health as related to quality of life (HRQoL), particularly for stroke patients. The evaluation was performed for three areas: 1) physical (energy, self-care, mobility, extremity functionality, work, speech, sight), 2) mental (personality, mood, thinking) and 3) social (social role, role of the family) (Williams et al., 1999a; Williams et al., 1999b).

## Statistical analysis
Statistics were analysed using SPSS Statistics 19. A sample calculation was performed, considering a confidence level of 95% at α = 0.05 and a test power at 1-β = 0.80. Sample size calculations were used to estimate the frequency in population along with the finite population correction factor (FPC) (Chow et al., 2008). The following formula was used:

n = N • X / X + N - 1

where X = Z Ա / 2 2 ∗ p ∗ 1 - p MO E 2X = Z² α/2 •p •(1-p)/MOE², and Z² α/2 is the critical value of the normal distribution at α/2 (e.g. for a confidence level of 95%, α is 0.05 and the critical value is 1.96), MOE is the margin of error, p is the sample proportion, and N is the population size. According to this formula, the sample size should be higher or equal to 70.

Initially, over 300 patients were enrolled in this study, yet only 85 had a complete dataset, among which 15 were incompatible with the requirements of our follow up study (they had some medical boundaries). Thus, the current sample has 70 patients, divided into 3 subgroups.

Average parameter values, frequency ranges, standard deviations, statistical significance tests using the ANOVA method and z-statistic were calculated. ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni) was used to analyze the differences among groups for evaluations, where the compared data were expressed as an average, and z-statistic was used to evaluate the spasticity, where the data compared were expressed as percentage. Statistical significance was considered at p < 0.05. To assess the sensitivity to change of the measure, the statistical effect size (ES) system was used. ES interpretation was compiled as: 1) small ES = 0.20; 2) medium ES = 0.50; and 3) large ES = 0.80. This system is relevant in presenting the findings of a quantitative study (an effect can be identified by a p-value, but this p-value cannot reveal its magnitude) (Sullivan and Feinn, 2012). Calculation of the ES is performed by using the following equation: ES = m 1 - m 2 / s 1 , where m1 is the average value of initial score, m2 is the average score value after a determined period, and s1 is the standard deviation value of initial score.

## Patient characteristics
In terms of demographic and clinical characteristics, no statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups (Table I ).

## Motor deficiency evaluation - Barthel Index
The Barthel Index evolution exhibits statistically significant difference among all groups as assessed by one-way ANOVA (F = 4.766, p = 0.012 for BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin and F = 5.741, p = 0.006 for BFT + Lokomat group, and F = 3.122, p = 0.049 for BFT group). ANOVA analysis revealed no consistent differences in the Barthel Index among the groups at 6 or 12 months.

In the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group, the motor deficiency disappeared in 9.09% of patients in the first 6 months, and 9.09% in the next 6 months, while in patients with very severe or severe deficiency, it became moderate or mild after 12 months, in 22.72% of patients (13.63% for the first 6 months and 9.09% for the next 6 months). The Barthel Index mean thus increased from 51.14 at the beginning to 59.77 at 6 months (p = 0.232) and to 65.91 at 12 months (p = 0.009). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the motor deficiency disappeared in 5.56% of patients in the first 6 months, and 5.56% in the next 6 months, while in patients with severe or very severe deficiency, it became moderate or mild after 12 months in 16.67% of patients (11.12% in the first 6 months and 5.56% in the next 6 months), the Barthel Index mean rising from 51.33 initially to 60.28 at 6 months (p = 0.152) and to 66.39 at 12 months (p = 0.004). In the BFT group, the motor deficiency disappeared in 6.67% of patients in the first 6 months and in 3.33% in the next 6 months, while in patients with very severe or severe initial deficiency it became moderate or mild after 12 months in 10.0% of patients (6.67% in the first 6 months and 3.33% in the next 6 months, the Barthel Index mean increasing from 50.50 at the beginning to 55.67 at 6 months (p = 0.513) and 59.83 at 12 months (p = 0.044). The best ES was recorded in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (Table II ). ANOVA analysis revealed no consistent differences in the Barthel Index among the groups at 6 or 12 months.

Since the Lokomat procedure led to good results, a risk analysis was performed in order to assess if the observed improvements could be considered statistically significant. Thus, the calculated values, both the risk ratio (RR) and odds ratio (OR) indicators were computed with a confidence interval of 95%. Three different scenarios can be described: 1) when comparing the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group to the BFT group, 2) when comparing the BFT + Lokomat group to the BFT group, and 3) the overall study (when were considered only two groups: with or without the Lokomat procedure run on the patients). In the first and second scenario, a protective risk factor (RR, OR < 1) was obtained, yet with no statistic significance (p > 0.05). However, a significant risk factor was found (RR = 0.66, 95% (0.5; 0.88), OR = 0.16, 95% (0.04; 0.64), p = 0.006 < 0.05) when the entire group with the Lokomat procedure (with or without Cerebrolysin) was compared to the group with only BFT. These results were obtained by running a contingency table with the following proportions: 40% of the patients with the Lokomat procedure + the BFT procedure (N1 = 40 patients) had shown major improvements, compared with the group of patients with only BFT procedure (N2 = 30 patients), where only 10% showed improvements. The p value was obtained using a Chi-square test for proportions, thus inferring that the Lokomat procedure provides a reliable improvement for all patients.

## Spasticity assessment Ashworth Scale
Data regarding the evolution of spasticity, measured with the Ashworth scale are presented in Table III . Regardless of the assessment, Z - statistical analysis showed that no significant differences were observed (p > 0.05) between the groups with associated therapy related to the BFT group.

At 12 months, the percentage of patients with a score ≥ 2 decreased by 31.82% in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (18.18% in the first 6 months, and 13.04% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.016), by 27.78% in the BFT + Lokomat group (16.67% in the first 6 months and 11.11% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.057) and by 6.67% in the BFT group (in the first 6 months and 3.33% over the next 6 months) (p = 0.595) (Fig. 1 ).

## Functional independence evaluation - FIM Scale
Evolution of the functional independence was statistically significant for all studied groups, total FIM and for both domains of FIM scale, as determined by one-way ANOVA: → total FIM: F = 10.840, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 9.238, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 12.958, p < 0.001 for BFT group, → motor score: F = 15.217, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 7.930, p = 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 7.684, p = 0.001 for BFT group, and → cognitive score: F = 4.737 p = 0.012 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 5.259, p = 0.008 for BFT + Lokomat; and F = 4.770, p = 0.011 for BFT group.

Compared to the baseline assessment, the FIM score for BFT+ Lokomat+Cerebrolysin group increased from 87.68 to 99.09 at 6 months (p = 0.016) and at 12 months to 105.77 (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 60.36 to 68.77 at 6 months (p = 0.002) and at 12 months to 73.05 (p < 0.001); and the cognition score increased from 27.32 to 30.32 at 6 months (p = 0.300) and at 12 months to 105.77 (p = 0.009).

For the BFT + Lokomat group, compared to the baseline assessment, the FIM score increased from 88.23 to 98.24 at 6 months (p = 0.55) and to 104.88 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.23 to 66.52 at 6 months (p = 0.079) and at 12 months to 70.94 (p = 0.001); and the cognition score increased from 29.00 to 31.72 at 6 months (p = 0.242) and at 12 months to 33.94 (p = 0.001).

In the BFT group the FIM score increased from 88.28 to 96.95 at 6 months (p = 0.005), and to 100.85 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.06 to 65.17 at 6 months (p = 0.040) and at 12 months to 67.68 (p = 0.001), while the cognition score increased from 29.22 to 31.78 at 6 months (p = 0.159) and at 12 months to 33.17 (p = 0.009). ANOVA analysis revealed no significant differences in FIM score among the groups at 6 and at 12 months, but the best ES was recorded for the group combining all three associated therapies (Table IV ).

## Quality of life evaluation - SS-QOL Scale
ANOVA analysis showed a significant positive evolution for all three groups, across all three areas of the SS-QOL Scale and total, as follows: → physical score: F = 11.549, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 6.318, p = 0.004 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 11.617, p < 0.001 for BFT group, → mental score: F = 13.647, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 7.236, p = 0.002 for BFT + Lokomat; and F = 6.005, p = 0.004 for BFT group, → social score: F = 8.813, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 8.031, p = 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; and F = 10.724, p < 0.001 for BFT group, and → SS-SQL: F = 21.217, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 11.358, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 17.097, p < 0.001for BFT group.

As for the physical score, in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group, it increased from 106.18 to 118.41 at 6 months (p = 0.024) and to 127.50 at 12 months (p < 0.001). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the score increased from 106.11 to 117.50 at 6 months (p = 0.107) and to 124.72 at 12 months (p = 0.003), while in the BFT group it increased from 106.03 to 115.90 at 6 months (p = 0.100) and to 121.67 at 12 months (p < 0.001).

In the mental domain, in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group the score increased from 23.77 to 28.18 at 6 months (p = 0.024) and to 32.27 at 12 months (p < 0.001). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the score increased from 23.94 to 28.06 at 6 months (p = 0.099) and to 31.06 at 12 months (p = 0.001), while in the BFT group it increased from 23.67 to 25.70 at 6 months (p = 0.365) and to 28.17 at 12 months (p = 0.003).

In the social domain, in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group the score increased from 16.18 to 18.14 at 6 months (p = 0.039) and to 19.36 at 12 months (p < 0.001). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the score increased from 15.61 to 17.83 at 6 months (p = 0.045) and to 19.11 at 12 months (p = 0.001), while in the BFT group it increased from 16.10 to 17.63 at 6 months (p = 0.042) and to 18.93 at 12 months (p < 0.001). The highest ES was obtained in the group that combined all three therapies (Table V ).

ANOVA analysis revealed a significant improvement at 6 months in the mental score of the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group versus the BFT group (p = 0.024). After 12 months, the difference became significant in both groups with Lokomat versus BFT group (p = 0.002, respectively p = 0.015). In addition, the SS-SQL total score was significantly higher at 12 months for the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group than the BFT group (p = 0.040).

## Discussion
Recovery from and assistance with neurological problems are long-term processes that may sometimes last for the rest of the patient's life. Stroke patients often suffer from sequels such as sensory impairments, perceptual deficiencies, balance deficiency, depression, aphasia, dementia, paralysis and degeneration of cognitive functions, all of which may persist for years (Brewer et al., 2013).

Even with optimal care in specialized units, less than a third of patients who have suffered a stroke fully recover (The Atlnatis et al., 2004). Post-stroke recovery is made through a complex and individualized plan, unlimited in time, that begins at the intensive care unit and continues in a medical recovery clinic or at the patient's home. Rehabilitation aims to give people with disabilities the opportunity to maintain their physical, intellectual, mental and social functions at an optimal level (International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, 2014). A meta-analysis shows that continuous rehabilitation efforts after discharge, within the first year of stroke onset, reduce a patient's functional impairment (Legg et al., 2004). As a result of recovery therapies, 80% of patients recover partially and 10% recover completely, while 10% remain in the vegetative stage (Sullivan et al., 1982).

In this study of stroke patients, the evolution of their motor deficiency, spasticity, functional independence and quality of life were compared according to the specific therapies associated with the classic recovery program. The recovery program aimed at improving the functional status, reducing motor deficiency, diminishing patient dependency, preventing and combatting complications, family and socio-professional reinsertion. An approach combining Lokomat training, neuroprotection, and classic recovery therapy was attempted so as to identify therapeutic regimens that could be applied in the first year following a stroke, in order to increase functional independence and the patient's quality of life, as well as to augment chances of complete rehabilitation.

Lokomat is a device successfully used for locomotor deficiency recovery, mainly used in acute and sub-acute phases. Data from the literature concerning walking parameters, though showing differing results, suggest the use of the Lokomat even for the patients' chronic neurological and post-stroke impairments (Hidler et al., 2009a, 2009b; Hornby et al., 2008; Kelley et al., 2013). A pilot case study conducted in 2014 showed that motor function, balance, muscle force and gait, as well as cognition, mood and related strategies may all be successfully improved by robot-assisted training (Calabrò et al., 2014).

The combination of Lokomat training, Cerebrolysin treatment and standard rehabilitation therapy in post-stroke treatment has shown additional benefits for the rehabilitation of the patients in this study. In terms of motor function, as assessed by measuring the Barthel Index, the best results were obtained in the early stages of rehabilitation, when Lokomat treatment was associated with classic recovery therapy and neurotrophic medication. The most important benefits were improved walking independence, muscle tone, gait/walking speed and mobility. In a study on 146 patients treated with Cerebrolysin, significant improvements in the Barthel Index were observed at the end of the treatment period, with the effect lasting for 3 months after the beginning of treatment (Ladurner et al., 2005).

Robotic assistance eliminates prolonged repetitive movements from post-stroke gait training with a physical therapist (Mayr et al., 2007). This study shows that, by combining the three therapies, the beneficial effects on the motor deficit of post stroke patients may be increased.

The spasticity that occurs post stroke, followed by superior motor neuron syndrome (lack of coordination, agonist/antagonist contraction and exhaustion) (Francisco and McGuire, 2012) was significantly reduced in all groups. The greatest decrease was recorded at the 6-month evaluation in the group where robotic care was combined with both neurotrophic medication and classic recovery treatment. A decrease in abnormal reflex rigidity following Lokomat training has also been observed in other studies (Mirbagheri et al., 2005). Data from the present study demonstrated that joining Lokomat with Cerebrolysin and classic recovery resulted in a faster decrease in spasticity, as determined by the Ashworth Index, in post-stroke patient's recovery.

Functional independence, measured with the FIM scale in this study, evolved positively in all three groups, showing significant improvement in the motor, cognition and overall scores, consistent with other studies (Dundar et al., 2014; Esclarín-Ruz et al., 2014; Mirbagheri et al., 2005). In this case as well, the best effects were obtained by associating the three therapies. These results show that the combination of the studied therapies induces an increase in functional independence and a reduction of the time interval when the effects of therapy are established.

The quality of life was also positively influenced, irrespective of the treatments applied, in all three areas: physical, mental and social, with the greatest impact noted for the mental. The evolution was significantly better in all groups, with the best results in the group that included neurotrophic medication. This may be explained by the fact that, mentally, the patient feels more comfortable when involved in several recovery activities, thus leading to a favourable evolution in rehabilitation.

Rehabilitation of the post-stroke patients should include several therapeutic directions in order to identify treatment regimens that can turn disabilities into abilities. In the present study, a more correct and beneficial approach of neuroprotection and recovery was attempted. This study is significant in that it monitors the effects obtained by associating robotic training with classic recovery treatment and neurotrophic medication, administered over time, for parameters that concern both physical and neurological evolution of patients in post-stroke treatment for up to 12 months. Though favourable evidence emerged from the benefits of Cerebrolysin (as a neurotrophic factor), combined with Lokomat treatment (robotic orthosis for walking rehabilitation) and classic medical recovery, a thorough, longer-term study involving several patients would definitely be useful to establish a more precise therapeutic scheme with a role in early recovery of deficiencies and disabilities occurring following a stroke.

## Conclusions
The association of neurotrophic treatment, Lokomat training and classic recovery techniques leads to improvements in motor deficiency, evolution of spasticity, functional independence, and quality of life. All of these indices showed improvement in the Cerebrolysin + Lokomat + BFT group compared to other therapies. The results of this study confirm the importance of recovery treatment post stroke, as well as the importance of following a specific schedule in order to achieve favourable results in improving patients' functional status.

headline.statement: Ten of the 27 FIM means in Table IV cannot be the average of any set of whole-number scores from the group sizes the paper states, and all ten fall in the two comparison groups while the Cerebrolysin group's nine means all check out.
headline.evidence: Group II (n = 18): "the FIM score increased from 88.23 to 98.24 at 6 months (p = 0.55) and to 104.88 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.23 to 66.52 at 6 months (p = 0.079)". Group III (n = 30): "In the BFT group the FIM score increased from 88.28 to 96.95 at 6 months (p = 0.005), and to 100.85 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.06 to 65.17 at 6 months (p = 0.040) and at 12 months to 67.68 (p = 0.001), while the cognition score increased from 29.22 to 31.78 at 6 months (p = 0.159)". For n = 30 a mean must be a whole number divided by 30: the nearest reachable values to 88.28 are 88.27 and 88.30; to 96.95 they are 96.93 and 96.97; to 100.85 they are 100.83 and 100.87. Every one of these ten values is printed twice in the article, once in Table IV and once in the Results prose.
headline.plain: The paper reports average disability scores for three groups of patients. Those scores are whole numbers for each patient, so any group average has to be a whole number divided by the number of patients in that group. Ten of the reported averages are not -- there is no combination of patient scores in a group of 18 or 30 that would produce them. All ten belong to the two groups the treatment was compared against; the treatment group's own figures are all reachable.

findings.title: Ten Table IV FIM means unreachable from any sample of the stated group size
findings.location: Table IV (Evolution of the FIM score), Motor / Cognition / Total rows for BFT + Lokomat (n = 18) and BFT (n = 30); the same ten values also appear in Results, FIM Scale, paras 3-4
findings.reported: Table IV prints 27 mean +/- dispersion cells across three groups. For n = 18: 59.23, 66.52, 88.23, 98.24. For n = 30: 29.22, 31.78, 67.68, 88.28, 96.95, 100.85.
findings.computed: All ten fail GRIM with failure_mode 'granularity'. Re-run in this stage on the six n = 30 cells via check_table: 18 of 18 checks returned impossible, 0 refused (GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE each). Example: for n = 30 the nearest integer sum to 88.28 is 2648, giving 88.266667, which does not round back to 88.28. R `scrutiny` was run independently on 59.23/n=18, 88.28/n=30 and 100.85/n=30 and returned inconsistent for all three; the sweep had separately confirmed 59.23/18, 88.23/18, 29.22/30 and 96.95/30 against the same engine. Both engines agree on every value cross-checked. The corresponding nine means for the Cerebrolysin group (n = 22) all pass.
findings.assumptions: GRIM here requires only that each patient's FIM score is a whole number and that the mean was taken over the group size printed in the table header. The paper states FIM items are scored on 'a decreasing scale in 7 stages, from 7 (totally independent) to 1 (totally dependent)', so the summed scores are integers; the group sizes n = 22 / 18 / 30 are stated in the table headers and in the Study design. The failure mode returned is granularity, which does NOT depend on the assumed 13-91 / 5-35 / 18-126 scale limits, so rulebook rule 4's cap does not apply. The single benign explanation that would dissolve this finding is per-timepoint missing data making the true denominator smaller than the printed n -- but the paper reports no attrition and states the analytic sample had complete datasets. Extraction error is effectively excluded: the sweep reconciled Table IV against the PDF version of record cell by cell, all ten values are printed a second time in the Results prose, and this stage re-pulled the table independently.

consequence.explanation: Table IV is the only source in the paper for every FIM figure, so the nine reported FIM ANOVAs and the stated conclusion that 'the best ES was recorded for the group combining all three associated therapies' rest on numbers that cannot have come from the samples described.

findings.plain: Each patient's functional-independence score is a whole number, so a group average has to be that group's total divided by the number of patients -- for 30 patients, only certain two-decimal values are possible. Ten reported averages are not among them, meaning no group of the stated size could have produced them. Two independent statistical packages agree. All ten belong to the two groups used for comparison; the group that received the drug has no such problem, which is the reverse of what a simple typesetting accident would look like.

findings.title: Every ANOVA F statistic tested irreconcilable with the means and standard deviations printed beside it
findings.location: Results: Barthel Index para 1, FIM Scale para 1, SS-QOL Scale para 1; inputs from Tables II, IV and V
findings.reported: 24 F statistics, none with degrees of freedom. Barthel Group I: 'F = 4.766, p = 0.012'. Barthel control: 'F = 3.122, p = 0.049'. SS-QOL total Group I: 'F = 21.217, p < 0.001'.
findings.computed: Three F values re-tested in this stage, all outside the interval reachable from the paper's own printed means and SDs, with a Monte Carlo exact-match rate of 0 over 5,000 draws of the rounding box. Barthel Group I (means 51.14/59.77/65.91, SDs 9.36/10.22/10.82, n = 22 each): achievable F [11.732, 11.783], reported 4.766; achievable p [4.50e-05, 4.67e-05], reported 0.012. Barthel control (means 50.50/55.67/58.83, SDs 10.14/11.11/11.74, n = 30 each): achievable F [4.359, 4.387], reported 3.122; achievable p [0.0153, 0.0157], reported 0.049. SS-QOL total Group I (means 146.14/164.73/179.14, SDs 17.69/18.32/18.64, n = 22 each): achievable F [18.120, 18.158], reported 21.217. The sweep tested five and all five failed.
findings.assumptions: The recomputation treats each within-group time effect as the one-way ANOVA over three timepoints that the paper says it ran, and treats the tabulated dispersions as SDs. Two alternative readings were considered and neither rescues the pattern: a repeated-measures analysis removes between-subject error and would RAISE F, but four of the five misses are in the direction of the reported F being too SMALL; reading the dispersion as the SEM that Table II's row label states would LOWER F drastically (roughly 0.5 for Barthel Group I), but one miss is in the direction of the reported F being too LARGE. No single explanation covers both directions. For three of the FIM recomputations the input means are themselves among the ten GRIM failures above, so those inputs are already in question.

consequence.explanation: The 24 F statistics are the paper's entire evidence that 'Evolution of the functional independence was statistically significant for all studied groups' and that quality of life improved significantly in all three arms; whether any of them crosses the paper's alpha cannot be settled, because under the SD reading the true p-values are smaller than printed and under the SEM reading several would become non-significant.

findings.plain: For each outcome the paper reports a test statistic summarising how much scores changed over 12 months. That statistic can be recalculated from the averages and spreads printed in the same tables. Every one recalculated -- five by the initial sweep, three re-checked here -- comes out to a different number than the paper reports, and the mismatches go in both directions, so no single mistake such as using the wrong kind of test explains them. Because the paper never states how many patients and groups fed each test, there is no other way to check them.

findings.title: Spasticity decrement of 13.04% not a possible share of 22 patients, and it does not sum to the stated total
findings.location: Results, Spasticity assessment Ashworth Scale, para 2
findings.reported: "the percentage of patients with a score >= 2 decreased by 31.82% in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (18.18% in the first 6 months, and 13.04% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.016)"
findings.computed: Re-run in this stage: 13.04% of n = 22 implies 2.8688 patients. The reachable values around it are 9.09 (2/22), 13.64 (3/22) and 18.18 (4/22). Separately, the two components sum to 31.22, not the stated 31.82, a gap of 0.60 against a rounding tolerance of 0.015. Substituting the reachable neighbour 13.64 reproduces the stated total exactly, and Table III's counts for this group (9 -> 5 -> 2 of 22) give decrements of 18.18 and 13.64 points.
findings.assumptions: Requires only that a count of patients out of the stated 22 is a whole number; n = 22 is stated in the Study design and in every table header. The likeliest explanation by some distance is a transposition of 13.64 to 13.04 in a single sentence, which both the summation and Table III's own counts point to.

consequence.explanation: Affects the arithmetic of one descriptive sentence only; the direction and reported significance of the Group I spasticity change rest on Table III's counts and on p = 0.016, neither of which depends on this decomposition.

findings.plain: The paper says the share of patients with high muscle stiffness fell by 18.18% and then a further 13.04%, totalling 31.82%. With 22 patients, a percentage has to be a whole number of patients out of 22, and 13.04% is not -- it works out to 2.87 people. It is also 0.6 short of adding up to the stated total. Using 13.64% instead, which is exactly 3 of 22, makes both problems vanish and matches the counts in the paper's own table, so this looks like a typing slip rather than anything more. It changes nothing else in the paper.

findings.title: Bonferroni correction claimed in the Methods but reported p-values match uncorrected tests
findings.location: Methods, Statistical analysis; Results, SS-QOL Scale, final paragraph; means and SDs from Table V
findings.reported: Methods: "ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni) was used to analyze the differences among groups". Results: SS-QOL total higher in Group I than control at 12 months, p = 0.040; mental score p = 0.024 at 6 months and p = 0.002 at 12 months.
findings.computed: The sweep recomputed both from Table V as ordinary two-sample t-tests. SS-QOL total (179.14 +/- 18.64, n = 22 vs 168.77 +/- 16.44, n = 30): Welch p = 0.0435, Student p = 0.0387 against a reported 0.040. SS-QOL mental (32.27 +/- 4.28, n = 22 vs 28.17 +/- 3.11, n = 30): Welch p = 0.00051, Student p = 0.00021 against a reported 0.002. The reported values track the uncorrected comparison. multiplicity_report was run four times across the two stages -- three by the sweep, once here with the correction field omitted -- and returned n_tests = 0 every time, so the number of claims that would not survive correction could not be computed.
findings.assumptions: That the three group contrasts (I vs III, II vs III, I vs II) form one family per outcome, which is what the Methods' own reference to a Bonferroni post-hoc implies. I did not compute an adjusted threshold by hand; the tool that does that arithmetic refused, and this finding rests only on the tool-computed observation that the printed p-values match the uncorrected tests.

consequence.explanation: The paper's only direct between-group superiority claims -- that quality of life was better in the Cerebrolysin arm than in the control arm at 6 and 12 months -- are the ones closest to the 0.05 threshold, and whether they survive the correction the Methods claim was applied could not be determined because the multiplicity tool would not run.

findings.plain: When several comparisons are made on the same patients, the usual safeguard is to demand stronger evidence from each one, and the paper says it used such a safeguard. But the reported significance values match what you get without it. The paper's central claim -- that the drug group did better than the control group on quality of life -- is reported at a value just inside the usual cutoff, so it is exactly the kind of result the safeguard exists to catch. We could not compute how many of these claims would survive, because the tool for that arithmetic would not run on this input.

findings.title: Statement that no baseline characteristic differed contradicted by the sex split in Table I
findings.location: Table I, Gender rows; claim in Results, Patient characteristics, and in Study design
findings.reported: "In terms of demographic and clinical characteristics, no statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups (Table I )." Table I: Females 3 (13.64%), 3 (16.67%), 14 (46.67%); Males 19 (86.36%), 15 (83.33%), 16 (53.33%).
findings.computed: Re-run in this stage on the counts re-read from Table I: chi-squared = 8.4679, df = 2, p = 0.0145. Expected female counts under no difference would be 6.29, 5.14 and 8.57 against observed 3, 3 and 14.
findings.assumptions: Table I prints no per-row p-values, so this is a recomputation against a blanket claim rather than a disagreement with a stated statistic. Note that allocation here was explicitly NOT random -- 'Patients ... were distributed among the 3 groups considering the selection method for each group along with to the patient's history, associated pathologies, clinical characteristics, and the signed consent for training with Lokomat' -- so an imbalance is expected. What is flagged is the claim that none exists, not the imbalance itself. For the same reason the baseline-uniformity tests (csf_test, bayesian_table1_dispersion) were deliberately not run: they ask whether groups are MORE alike than random allocation permits, and that null does not apply to a non-randomised study.

consequence.explanation: Every between-group comparison in the paper assumes the arms were comparable, and no outcome analysis adjusts for sex, so a control arm that is 47% female against 14% and 17% in the treated arms is an uncontrolled difference the paper states does not exist.

findings.plain: The paper says the three groups were alike at the start. They were not alike in one respect that it prints itself: the comparison group was about 47% women, the two treated groups about 14% and 17%. A difference that large would not usually arise by chance. Patients were not assigned to groups at random -- they were placed by their medical history and willingness to use the robot -- so an imbalance is unsurprising; the problem is the flat statement that there was none, combined with the fact that no later analysis adjusts for it.

findings.title: Dispersion labelled SEM in Table II, unlabelled in Tables IV and V, and used as a standard deviation
findings.location: Table II row label 'Mean +/- SEM'; Tables IV and V, all '+/-' cells; Methods, effect-size definition
findings.reported: Table II: "Mean +/- SEM  51.14 +/- 9.36". Methods: "ES = m1 - m2/s1, where ... s1 is the standard deviation value of initial score." Tables IV and V print '+/-' with no SD or SEM designation in caption, header or footnote.
findings.computed: Taken as an SD, 9.36 at n = 22 implies a standard error of 2.00 and sits at 18% of the ceiling for a 0-100 instrument. Taken as the SEM the label states, it implies an SD of 43.9, which is 86% of that ceiling. The tool's likely interpretation is SD. The effect sizes printed in Table II are reproduced by dividing the mean change by the tabulated dispersion, which is what the paper's own formula does with an SD.
findings.assumptions: The 0-100 Barthel range used for the plausibility ceiling is MY assumption, not the paper's -- the paper describes the instrument only as testing '10 stages for using the 10 ADL for self-care'. Per rulebook rule 4 this caps the severity at suspicious and disqualifies it as a headline. The likeliest explanation is simple mislabelling of the row: Olsen (2002) found 40% of studies reporting 'SD' had reported the standard error, and the same confusion in reverse is entirely ordinary. But the paper never resolves it, and the consequence is not cosmetic.

consequence.explanation: All 52 effect sizes in Tables II, IV and V, and every ANOVA recomputation, depend on whether the printed '+/-' value is a standard deviation or a standard error; under the SEM reading the paper's effect sizes would be roughly 4.7 times smaller, turning the 'large' effects its conclusions rest on into small ones.

findings.plain: The tables print a number after each average that describes how spread out the patients were. One table labels it as one kind of spread measure, the other two label it as nothing at all, and the paper's own effect-size formula treats it as a third thing. These differ by a factor of about five at these sample sizes. If the label on the first table is taken at face value, the paper's headline finding of large treatment effects becomes a finding of small ones. The most likely explanation is a mislabelled row -- a very common slip -- but as printed the reader cannot tell which reading is intended.

findings.title: Results text disagrees with the tables it summarises in two places
findings.location: Results, Barthel Index para 2 vs Table II; Results, FIM Scale para 2 vs Table IV
findings.reported: Text: "the Barthel Index mean increasing from 50.50 at the beginning to 55.67 at 6 months (p = 0.513) and 59.83 at 12 months (p = 0.044)" against Table II's "58.83 +/- 11.74". Text: "the cognition score increased from 27.32 to 30.32 at 6 months (p = 0.300) and at 12 months to 105.77 (p = 0.009)" against Table IV's cognition value of 32.73.
findings.computed: Re-read at source in this stage: Table II prints 58.83 +/- 11.74 for the control group at 12 months, a difference of exactly 1.0 from the text. Table IV prints 32.73 for Group I cognition at 12 months; the value 105.77 given in the text is that group's TOTAL FIM score at 12 months, quoted two sentences earlier in the same paragraph. A FIM cognition subscale cannot reach 105.77 under any of the instrument's definitions. The sweep confirmed both against the PDF version of record, so neither is an extraction artefact.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The sweep notes that Table II's 58.83 is the value consistent with the effect size of 0.82 printed in the same row under the paper's stated formula, which points to the table rather than the text being right in that instance.

consequence.explanation: The reported p = 0.044 for the control group's 12-month Barthel change is attached to whichever of 59.83 and 58.83 is correct and the reader cannot tell which; separately, a primary outcome sentence reports a cognition score that is in fact the total score.

findings.plain: In two places the numbers in the running text do not match the numbers in the tables they describe. One is a one-point difference in the comparison group's mobility score. The other is larger: the text says the thinking-and-communication score reached 105.77, but the table gives 32.73, and 105.77 is the overall score quoted two sentences earlier -- the subscale cannot reach that value at all. Both appear the same way in the published PDF, so these are errors in the article rather than in our reading of it. Neither changes a conclusion, but together they suggest the results text was not checked against the tables.

findings.title: Three measurements on the same patients analysed as a one-way ANOVA across independent groups
findings.location: Methods, Statistical analysis; Results, all within-group time effects
findings.reported: "ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni) was used to analyze the differences among groups for evaluations, where the compared data were expressed as an average", and every within-group time effect is described as 'one-way ANOVA' over baseline, 6 months and 12 months.
findings.computed: No arithmetic tool applies. Baseline, 6-month and 12-month scores are three measurements on the SAME 22 / 18 / 30 patients, which violates the independence assumption a one-way ANOVA requires; a repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed model is the matching analysis. Direction of the resulting bias: treating correlated measurements as independent inflates the error term and makes the test conservative, so this does not on its own explain the F discrepancies in finding 2, four of five of which run the other way.
findings.assumptions: Rulebook rule 5 (design validity). This is a reading of the Methods, not a recomputation, and the severity reflects that. Related reporting gaps recorded here rather than as separate findings: allocation was explicitly non-random, there is no trial registration number, no CONSORT flow diagram, and no adverse-event reporting for a 12-month intravenous drug protocol.

consequence.explanation: All 24 within-group time effects -- the paper's evidence that each therapy produced significant improvement -- use a test that does not match the repeated-measures structure of the data.

findings.plain: The same patients were measured three times, at the start, at six months and at a year. The paper analyses those three sets of measurements as though they came from three different groups of people, which is not the right test for repeated measurements on the same individuals. The correct test would normally make the results look stronger, not weaker, so this is a methodological mismatch rather than an explanation of the other problems -- but it means the reported comparisons were not computed the way the design required.

findings.title: Sample-size formula containing no power term presented as delivering 80% power
findings.reported: "A sample calculation was performed, considering a confidence level of 95% at alpha = 0.05 and a test power at 1-beta = 0.80 ... n = N * X / X + N - 1 ... where X = Z^2 alpha/2 * p * (1-p) / MOE^2 ... According to this formula, the sample size should be higher or equal to 70."
findings.computed: verify_power_analysis returned indeterminate: the calculation cannot be reproduced because no effect size is stated. Beyond that, the formula the paper prints is the standard expression for estimating a PROPORTION in a finite population to a given margin of error. It contains no beta and no power term, so it cannot yield '1-beta = 0.80', and the paper states neither the proportion p, nor the margin of error MOE, nor the population size N that the formula requires.
findings.assumptions: The observation that the printed formula contains no power term is a reading of the Methods text, not a tool result; the tool result behind this finding is only the indeterminate verdict from the missing effect size. Also worth a reader's attention without any inference drawn: the required N derived from this formula (>= 70) exactly equals the number recruited (70).

consequence.explanation: No specific result depends on this, but the adequacy of the sample size cannot be assessed from anything the paper reports.

findings.plain: The paper says it worked out how many patients it needed to have an 80% chance of detecting a real effect. The formula it prints does something different -- it estimates how many people you need to measure a percentage to within a given margin of error -- and contains nothing corresponding to that 80%. It also leaves out three of the quantities the formula needs. So the stated justification for the sample size cannot be reproduced or checked.

findings.title: Between-group quality-of-life effect at or above the 95th percentile for clinical medicine
findings.location: Table V, Mental rows at 12 months, Group I versus Group III
findings.reported: Mental domain at 12 months: 32.27 +/- 4.28 (n = 22) in the Cerebrolysin arm against 28.17 +/- 3.11 (n = 30) in the control arm. The paper's own within-group effect size for that cell is 2.11.
findings.computed: Cohen's d = 1.12, Hedges' g = 1.11 on a pooled SD of 3.65 with df = 50 -- at or above the 95th percentile of the tool's benchmark distribution for clinical medicine.
findings.assumptions: The benchmark percentiles the tool used (median 0.30, 75th 0.55, 95th 1.00) are flagged in its own output as an uncited estimate rather than a published table, so this is a soft comparison. Two of the three ordinary causes of an inflated effect cannot be excluded: the SD/SEM ambiguity in finding 6 (which would move the effect the other way) and the fact that the SS-QOL scoring range is never stated, so a scale mismatch cannot be ruled out. The third is ruled out -- the comparator is active (balneo-physiotherapy), not a waiting list. Severity is capped at suspicious; a large effect is unusual, never impossible.

consequence.explanation: Bears on the plausibility of the paper's central claim that adding Cerebrolysin to robotic gait training and physiotherapy produces a large quality-of-life advantage over physiotherapy alone.

findings.plain: The reported advantage of the drug group over the comparison group on the mental quality-of-life measure is larger than roughly 95% of effects reported in clinical medicine, from an add-on treatment tested against an active alternative rather than against nothing. That is not impossible and is not evidence of any error by itself, but it is unusual enough to warrant seeing the underlying data. The comparison benchmark used here is an estimate rather than a published reference table, so treat this as a soft signal.

findings.title: Degrees of freedom absent from all 24 reported F tests
findings.reported: "total FIM: F = 10.840, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 9.238, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 12.958, p < 0.001 for BFT group" -- the form used for all 24 F statistics.
findings.computed: statcheck extracted zero test statistics from the complete Results text. This is not a tool failure: every F is printed without degrees of freedom, and without them an F cannot be converted to a p-value, so no automated consistency check is possible. Verification of the F statistics therefore had to proceed indirectly, by recomputation from the group means and SDs (finding 2).
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own text. This is a refusal to judge, not a defect claim in itself -- but the omission is what forces every check of the paper's inferential statistics through the tables.
findings.reproduction: metascience statcheck --text "total FIM: F = 10.840, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 9.238, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 12.958, p < 0.001 for BFT group"

consequence.explanation: None of the 24 reported F tests can be checked by the standard automated route, so all verification of them depends on recomputation from tables whose own values are partly in question.

findings.plain: Whenever a paper reports this kind of test it should also report how many groups and how many patients went into it. This paper never does, in any of its 24 tests. Without those figures the reported result cannot be checked against the reported significance value by any standard method, and the only route left is to rebuild the test from the tables -- which is what was done, and which is where the mismatches in the second finding come from.

findings.title: Figure 1 caption grading p = 0.057 as 'weakly significant' against the paper's stated threshold of 0.05
findings.reported: Methods: "Statistical significance was considered at p < 0.05." Fig. 1 caption: "illustrates a highly statistically significant decrease (p=0.016) for the BFT+Lokomat+Cerebrolysin group, weakly significant (p=0.057) for the BFT+Lokomat group and not significant (p=0.595) for the BFT group."
findings.computed: No arithmetic is at issue -- the p-values themselves are printed consistently with the Results text. The defect is the verbal grading: 0.057 exceeds the single threshold the paper states, so by the paper's own rule the Group II spasticity result is not significant, and neither 'highly statistically significant' nor 'weakly significant' corresponds to any threshold the paper declares.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. The figure carries no values that are not already printed in Table III and the Results text, so nothing was lost by not reading the plotted bars.

consequence.explanation: Applying the paper's own stated threshold of p < 0.05 makes the Group II spasticity reduction non-significant, where the caption presents it as partially supporting the conclusion that Lokomat therapy reduces spasticity.

findings.plain: The paper states up front that it will call a result significant when its significance value is below 0.05. The figure caption then describes a value of 0.057 as 'weakly significant'. By the paper's own rule that result is simply not significant, so a null finding is being presented as partial support for the conclusion.

not_checked.location: Table II, Barthel Index means -- granularity at the instrument's true step size
not_checked.reason: The classic Barthel Index is scored in 5-point increments, so its true granularity is 5/n rather than 1/n. No tool in the suite accepts a step size other than 1, so only the weaker 1/n test could be run. The 27-of-27 clean result for Table II is therefore a weaker pass than the instrument would support.

not_checked.location: Effect-size column of Tables II, IV and V (52 ES values)
not_checked.reason: The paper defines its own effect size as ES = (m1 - m2)/s1, a within-group standardised change using the baseline SD. No validated tool implements that statistic -- check_effect_plausibility computes Cohen's d / Hedges' g from a pooled SD, a different quantity -- so the 52 printed ES values were not independently recomputed. Doing so would have required hand arithmetic, which is out of scope.

not_checked.location: Table I, baseline-similarity omnibus tests (csf_test, bayesian_table1_dispersion)
not_checked.reason: Deliberately not run, and this stage confirms that judgement. Both tests ask whether groups are MORE similar than random allocation allows; allocation here was explicitly non-random ('Patients ... were distributed among the 3 groups considering the selection method for each group along with to the patient's history, associated pathologies, clinical characteristics, and the signed consent for training with Lokomat'). Their null does not apply and running them would have manufactured a verdict.

not_checked.location: Multiplicity arithmetic for the between-group SS-QOL family and the within-group change family
not_checked.reason: multiplicity_report returned n_tests = 0 on four attempts across the two stages -- three by the sweep with and without an explicit correction field, and once in this stage with the field omitted entirely. The intended arithmetic never ran, so n_claims_lost_to_correction is undetermined. The paper runs 24 omnibus ANOVAs plus roughly 60 post-hoc and between-group comparisons on the same 70 patients and states a correction only within each ANOVA; that burden is therefore real but unquantified here. No hand substitute was computed.

not_checked.location: 19 of the 24 reported ANOVA F values
not_checked.reason: Eight F values were recomputed in total (five by the sweep, three re-checked in this stage) and every one fell outside its achievable range. The remaining 16 were not individually recomputed, for budget reasons. The tested set spans all three groups and three different instruments, so the pattern is unlikely to be confined to them, but that is an extrapolation and those values are formally unverified.

not_checked.location: Table V, Social rows: Group I and Group III at 6 months (SPRITE / GRIMMER)
not_checked.reason: Our SPRITE returned no_solution_proven and GRIMMER an independent sd_granularity failure for two cells, but the R cross-check did not confirm: rsprite2 raised a GRIMMER error rather than returning an infeasibility proof. Per the stage rule an errored cross-check yields indeterminate, so neither cell is reported as an anomaly. A further caveat that would apply even had it confirmed: the SS-QOL domain bounds were assumed (0-245), because the paper names the three domains without stating item counts or ranges.

not_checked.location: Four cells reproducible only under the population-SD convention (Table IV Cognition G1 baseline; Table V Social G1 12 months, Mental G2 baseline, Social G2 12 months)
not_checked.reason: Recorded but not raised to a finding. These are reproducible if the SD was computed with n rather than n-1 in the denominator -- the default in numpy and in Excel's STDEVP. That is a legitimate reporting choice, not evidence of anything, and the paper states no convention. It would only be odd because most cells in the same tables are consistent under the sample convention.

not_checked.location: All reported p-values -- GRIM-U rank-sum granularity
not_checked.reason: Deliberately not run. The paper attributes its p-values to ANOVA, chi-squared and a z-statistic for proportions; no Mann-Whitney or Wilcoxon test is reported. GRIM-U applies only to rank-sum p-values and applying it here is the tool's documented top false-accusation risk.

not_checked.location: Table I, binary demographic rows -- DEBIT
not_checked.reason: Not applicable. DEBIT requires a 0/1 variable reported as a mean with an SD; Table I reports binary characteristics as counts and percentages in separate columns, with no mean/SD pair.

The paper reports 'Z - statistical analysis showed that no significant differences were observed (p > 0.05)' without printing any z value, any per-comparison p, or which proportions were compared. There is nothing numeric to check, and absence_of_evidence could not be run because no confidence interval is given.

not_checked.location: The 6-month and 12-month between-group ANOVA claims for Barthel and FIM
not_checked.reason: Reported only as 'ANOVA analysis revealed no consistent differences ... at 6 or 12 months' with no F, no p and no interval. absence_of_evidence requires an interval and declines without one, so these null claims could not be tested for whether they actually rule out a meaningful effect.

not_checked.location: Individual verification of the ~180 count/percentage cell pairs in Tables I-III
not_checked.reason: Each printed percentage should equal 100 x count / n, but the counts and percentages sit in separate columns, so the typed parser reads them as independent bare numbers and check_table cannot pair them. Column-level structure was verified instead via 34 summation rows, all consistent; cell-level agreement was spot-verified only where a text claim depended on it.
None accompany this article; only the .xml and .pdf were present in the paper directory. This is 'not provided' rather than 'present but unreadable'.

limitations: FIGURES: this agent reads text and tables. No figure image was rendered or read in either stage of this review. The paper contains one figure, and its caption was read as text from page 6 of the PDF; the sweep recorded that Fig. 1 carries no values that are not already printed in Table III and the Results text, so no unique data were lost. Nothing in this report rests on reading a plotted mark.

Two of the four questions Heathers says a granularity or similarity result must be read against are outside this system's reach entirely: it reads one paper and reaches no network, so it cannot tell you whether similar patterns appear in other papers by these authors (the article itself cites Uivarosan et al., 2018 on the same topic), nor what the equivalent recomputed values look like in comparable stroke-rehabilitation trials. The interpretation of the Table IV granularity finding is therefore partly ours and partly the reader's.

The multiplicity arithmetic could not be obtained. multiplicity_report returned n_tests = 0 on four separate attempts across both stages, so no count of claims lost to correction backs finding 4; only the tool-computed observation that the reported p-values match uncorrected tests does. No hand-computed substitute was used.

A direct re-run of grim_check on individual Table IV means failed with a parameter-type error in the tool's decimals handling. Our engine's verdict was obtained instead through check_table, which routes the same GRIM implementation and returned impossible on 18 of 18 checks for the n = 30 block. This is a limitation of one calling path, not of the result, and R scrutiny was run independently on three of the same values.

The Barthel range of 0-100 used for the SD-versus-SEM plausibility ceiling, and the SS-QOL domain range of 0-245, are assumptions this reviewer supplied; the paper states neither. Both findings that depend on them are capped at suspicious and name the assumption, and neither is the headline.
Sixteen of the paper's 24 F statistics were not individually recomputed. The eight that were all failed, but the generalisation to the remainder is an extrapolation.

No raw or participant-level data accompany the article, so the duplication and reconstruction checks that work on raw data could not be attempted; the duplication analysis reported here operated on summary statistics only.

Table III (Evolution of the Ashworth Index) -- 126 cells; 8 summation rows, all consistent

questions_for_authors.question: Table IV reports FIM means of 88.28, 96.95 and 100.85 for the BFT group (n = 30) and 59.23, 66.52, 88.23 and 98.24 for the BFT + Lokomat group (n = 18). Because FIM scores are sums of whole-number item ratings, a mean over 30 patients must be a whole number divided by 30 -- the nearest reachable values to 88.28 are 88.27 and 88.30 -- and none of these ten values is reachable at the stated group size, while all nine means for the n = 22 group are. Could you confirm the number of patients contributing to each FIM cell at each timepoint, and say whether any FIM scores were prorated or imputed?
questions_for_authors.why: Directly tests the only benign explanation for the headline finding: that the effective denominator differs from the printed group size because of missing data at a timepoint.

questions_for_authors.question: The paper reports 24 F statistics without degrees of freedom. Recomputing three of them as the one-way ANOVAs the Results describe, from the means and SDs printed in the same tables, gives F between 11.73 and 11.78 for the Barthel Group I comparison against a reported 4.766; F between 4.36 and 4.39 for the Barthel control group against a reported 3.122; and F between 18.12 and 18.16 for the SS-QOL total in Group I against a reported 21.217. Could you supply the degrees of freedom and the SPSS output for these three tests?
questions_for_authors.why: The misses run in both directions, which excludes the tidy explanations (repeated-measures analysis, or SEM read as SD). The degrees of freedom alone would identify what was actually computed.

questions_for_authors.question: Table II labels its dispersion 'Mean +/- SEM' (for example 51.14 +/- 9.36 at n = 22), while Tables IV and V print '+/-' with no designation in the caption, header or footnote, and the Methods define the effect size as ES = (m1 - m2)/s1 'where s1 is the standard deviation value of initial score'. Are the tabulated dispersions standard deviations or standard errors of the mean?
questions_for_authors.why: The 52 printed effect sizes and every ANOVA recomputation differ by a factor of about 4.7 between the two readings; under the SEM reading the paper's 'large' effects become small ones.

questions_for_authors.question: Three values in the Results text do not match the tables: the control group's 12-month Barthel mean is given as 59.83 in the text but 58.83 in Table II; the Group I 12-month FIM cognition score is given as 105.77 in the text but 32.73 in Table IV (105.77 being that group's total FIM score, quoted two sentences earlier); and the Group I spasticity decrement of 13.04% is not a possible share of 22 patients, where 13.64% is exactly 3 of 22 and makes the components sum to the stated 31.82%. Which value is correct in each case?
questions_for_authors.why: Three localisable discrepancies, each with an identifiable likely correction, that a corresponding author can settle from the original output in one reply.

questions_for_authors.question: The Methods state that 'ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni)' was used for the between-group comparisons, but the reported values -- p = 0.040 for the SS-QOL total and p = 0.002 for the mental score, Group I versus control at 12 months -- reproduce as uncorrected two-sample tests from the Table V means and SDs (0.039 and 0.0002 pooled; 0.043 and 0.0005 Welch). Were the between-group p-values adjusted for the three group contrasts, and if so over what family?
questions_for_authors.why: Determines whether the paper's only direct superiority claims survive the correction its own Methods describe; the SS-QOL total claim sits just inside alpha.

input.report_markdown:
## What the paper claims

This is a non-randomised, three-arm comparative study of 70 Romanian stroke patients treated at two hospitals in Baile Felix and Oradea between 2011 and 2014. One group received balneo-physiotherapy plus Lokomat robotic gait training plus intravenous Cerebrolysin (n = 22), one received balneo-physiotherapy plus Lokomat (n = 18), and one balneo-physiotherapy alone (n = 30). Patients were assessed at baseline, 6 months and 12 months on the Barthel Index, the modified Ashworth scale, the FIM and the SS-QOL. The paper concludes that combining all three therapies improves motor deficiency, spasticity, functional independence and quality of life, with the best effect sizes in the three-therapy group.

## What verified, and why that matters here

A great deal of this paper checks out, and the clean parts are what make the unclean part legible. All nine Barthel mean cells in Table II pass every granularity test applied -- 27 of 27 checks, no refusals. Across Table V's 36 SS-QOL cells, not one mean fails: 100 of 108 checks are consistent, and the eight that are not are all on the dispersion side, four of them explained by the ordinary choice of dividing by n rather than n-1. Fifty-five of 56 sums reconcile: every category count in Tables I-III sums to its group size, FIM motor plus cognition reproduces FIM total in all nine cells, SS-QOL domains reproduce the total in all nine, and the sample flow adds up. Table I's hemiplegia block looks over-subscribed until you notice it is two nested classifications, and then it reconciles cleanly. The risk-analysis paragraph is the soundest piece of work in the article: the 2x2 rebuilt from its stated proportions reproduces the reported p = 0.006 under Fisher's exact test, and both the risk ratio and the odds ratio sit at their interval midpoints on the log scale with recovered p-values bracketing it. Across 1,728 cross-group comparisons of summary statistics, no identical mean/SD pair appears.

So this is not a paper where everything is broken. The problems are two, and both are sharply localised.

## The shape of the Table IV problem

Ten of Table IV's 27 FIM means cannot be produced by any set of whole-number scores from the group sizes the table itself prints. That verdict now rests on two independent implementations: our own engine returned impossible on 18 of 18 checks for the n = 30 block when re-run in this stage, and R's `scrutiny` package independently returned inconsistent for 59.23 at n = 18 and for 88.28 and 100.85 at n = 30. Extraction error, which the base rates say should be the first suspect, is about as thoroughly excluded as it can be: the sweep reconciled Table IV against the PDF of record cell by cell, this stage re-pulled the table, and every one of the ten values is printed a second time in the Results prose. A number that appears identically in two places in the published article is not an artefact of our reading it.

The distribution of the failures is the part worth putting to the authors. All ten sit in the two comparison groups. The Cerebrolysin group's nine FIM means are all reachable -- and reachable is a narrower condition at n = 22 than at n = 30, so the asymmetry is not an artefact of group size. I draw no conclusion from this; I note that the group whose superiority the paper concludes for is the group whose numbers survive the test, and that the modal innocent explanation -- missing data shrinking the true denominator below the printed n -- is one the authors can confirm or exclude in a sentence.

## The ANOVA problem reaches further

Eight F statistics were recomputed from the paper's own printed means and standard deviations; all eight fall outside the interval those inputs permit, with a Monte Carlo exact-match rate of zero. This is the finding with the widest reach, because it touches all four outcomes rather than one table. What makes it resistant to a benign reading is the direction: most reported values are too small, but the SS-QOL total is too large (21.217 against an achievable 18.12 to 18.16). A repeated-measures analysis -- which is what the design actually called for, since these are three measurements on the same patients -- would raise F systematically. Reading the dispersions as the SEM that Table II's row label states would lower F drastically. Neither covers both directions, and no combination of them does.

That SD-versus-SEM ambiguity is not a pedantic point. The paper's own effect-size formula divides by "the standard deviation value of initial score", the printed effect sizes are reproduced by dividing by the tabulated dispersion, and yet Table II calls that dispersion an SEM while Tables IV and V label it as nothing at all. Mislabelling is overwhelmingly the likeliest explanation -- Olsen found 40% of studies reporting "SD" had reported the standard error, and the reverse confusion is just as ordinary -- but the reader cannot tell, and all 52 effect sizes in the paper hinge on it.

## Reporting context

None of the following makes a number wrong, but together they bear on how much external checking this work received: allocation was explicitly non-random and the paper nonetheless states flatly that no baseline characteristic differed, when the sex split alone gives p = 0.0145; there is no trial registration, no CONSORT flow diagram, and no adverse-event reporting for a protocol delivering 120 days of intravenous Cerebrolysin per patient over a year; the study is declared to have received no external funding; and a clinical stroke-rehabilitation trial containing no environmental content appears in an environmental-science journal.

## Verdict

Ten reported averages in the functional-independence table cannot have come from the samples described, confirmed by two independent engines on values printed twice in the article; and not one of the eight test statistics recomputed from the paper's own tables can be reproduced. Those numbers are the paper's evidence for one of the four outcomes in its title and for all 24 of its significance tests. I do not think the reported results can be relied upon without the raw data being made available for reanalysis.
